title: The Drafty-Room Map: A Two-Person Brief for a Home Energy Assessment
subtitle: An additional WILDWIRE Daily Read: a practical way to turn everyday comfort concerns into useful questions for an energy professional.
imageAlt: Two friends at a kitchen table compare a simple floor plan marked with notes about rooms that feel cold, hot, or drafty.
imageConcept: a woman and a man who are partners, with grounded attainable appearances together, in a specific visual scene about “The Drafty-Room Map: A Two-Person Brief for a Home Energy Assessment”: Two housemates sit at a lived-in kitchen table with a hand-drawn floor plan, utility bills and pens, comparing notes about where the home feels uncomfortable.
body: Start with the rooms, not the remedy

A room that stays chilly, overheats in the afternoon or feels drafty near a window can become an invitation to buy a particular product. A more useful first step is to record what you notice before deciding what the cause—or the fix—must be. A professional home energy assessment can look at energy use and comfort concerns, and may use diagnostic tools such as a blower-door test or infrared scan. The assessment is meant to inform decisions, not to make every uncomfortable room evidence for one specific upgrade. The U.S. Department of Energy recommends preparing notes about comfort problems and recent energy bills; a brief room-by-room record gives those observations a place to start. [1]

This is not a do-it-yourself audit or a diagnosis of the building. It is a way to help an assessor understand how the home feels to the people who live in it, and to make the visit more focused.

Use a simple sketch, printed floor plan or list of rooms. Each person who wants to take part can separately note one or two places that feel different from the rest of the home. Add the time or conditions when the concern shows up: a bedroom feels cold overnight, a south-facing room becomes hot on sunny afternoons, or a draft is noticeable beside the back door when the wind picks up. If you do not know when it happens, write that down too.

Keep the wording close to what you can observe. “Cold near the floor on winter mornings” is more useful than “the insulation is bad,” because the first describes an experience while the second assumes a cause. Include rooms that feel comfortable as well as those that do not; that comparison may help the professional understand the pattern. The map can be rough. Its job is to preserve details you might not remember during a busy appointment.
Compare notes without arguing over the thermostat

Two people can experience the same home differently. One may notice a bedroom that feels cold at night; another may be comfortable there but bothered by glare and heat in the afternoon. Treat those differences as information rather than as a contest over who is right. Put both observations on the map, including who noticed them and when.

Before the visit, add practical context: how each room is used, whether doors are usually open or closed, and whether the concern is seasonal or happens year-round. If a room is used by someone with a particular comfort need, include that only if they want it recorded. The purpose is not to turn residents into data points, but to give the assessor a clearer account of how the home works for its household. A shared map can also keep one person’s long-standing concern from being lost in a conversation dominated by the most recent bill or the most obvious draft.

Alongside room notes, record visible details that may be relevant: condensation on a window, a damp-looking area, a door that does not close easily, or a noticeable temperature difference between adjoining spaces. Describe what you see and where. Do not try to determine the cause from appearance alone, and do not disturb materials or equipment to investigate. If a concern involves persistent moisture, a combustion appliance, unusual odors or another safety issue, mention it clearly and ask the assessor how it should be handled; an energy assessment is not a substitute for the right specialist evaluation.

Gather recent utility-bill summaries if they are easy to find. Bills can provide context about energy use over time, but they do not by themselves explain why a particular room feels uncomfortable. Note unusual circumstances that could affect comparisons, such as a change in household size or a period when the home was unoccupied. Keep the record concise: relevant context is helpful, but a stack of paperwork is not a prerequisite for asking for an assessment.
Ask what the assessment actually covers

“Home energy assessment” can describe different scopes of work. Before scheduling, ask what the professional will inspect, how long the visit usually takes, whether diagnostic testing is included, and what you should prepare. The Department of Energy describes a whole-house approach that considers the building envelope alongside heating and cooling, electrical systems and appliances; it also identifies health-and-safety checks such as combustion-appliance testing and ventilation assessment as relevant elements of weatherization work. That does not mean every assessor or every appointment includes every check. Ask what applies to the service you are considering. [2]

It is also reasonable to ask what the final report will contain, when you can expect it and whether there is a fee. Clarify whether recommendations are prioritized, whether proposed work is separate from the assessment, and whether you are being asked to make any commitment during the visit. These questions help you compare services on what they actually provide rather than on a broad label.
Read the report for evidence and estimates

A useful report should help you distinguish what the assessor observed or measured from what they recommend and what they estimate may happen after work is completed. Ask for that distinction in plain language. If a finding concerns a particular room, see whether the report explains how it connects to the proposed action. If savings are projected, ask what assumptions the estimate relies on and whether it accounts for the home’s actual use and energy costs.

 You do not need to accept every recommendation at once. A report is information to review, compare and discuss—not an instruction to replace equipment or begin a project immediately.

An assessment and a home-improvement sale are not the same thing. If an assessment leads to a proposal, take time to consider it. The Federal Trade Commission advises consumers to check licensing with the relevant state or county authority, obtain multiple written estimates and read contracts carefully; requirements vary by state. Be wary of pressure to sign quickly or promises that make savings sound guaranteed. [3]

Do not perform tests involving combustion appliances or change heating, cooling or ventilation settings as part of making your map. Leave technical testing to qualified professionals, and seek an appropriate specialist when a concern falls outside the assessor’s role. The goal is modest but worthwhile: describe what the household notices, find out what the assessment can establish, and decide what—if anything—to do with the findings at your own pace.
Leave the map with one question for the visit

At the next calm moment, choose a room that matters to someone who lives in the home and write one observation together: where it happens, when it tends to happen, and what the room is used for. Let each person add their own account without correcting the other’s. Then circle one question to bring to an assessor, such as, “What would help determine why this room feels colder than the others?” Keep the map with recent bill summaries if you have them, but leave blank spaces where details are unknown. The finished page is not a verdict on the house. It is a focused starting point for a conversation in which the household can ask what was measured, what remains uncertain and which next step, if any, feels right.
